doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

title: Over-analyzing solos
summary: Transcribing solos to death misses improvising as expression and getting from A to B.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. I agree. Sometimes you see in some of the magazines that you may have stopped reading, they analyze — they transcribe a solo and analyze it to death and every note has to have some function. Here’s what the player was probably thinking why he played this B flat. I’m just like well maybe he didn’t even mean to play that B flat.
It’s like he needed to keep playing.

That’s right. And that’s what happens so many times but you’re right. I mean sometimes a certain note or a group or notes has no agenda. Basically we forget that improvising, two things are happenings — of many things — but one we’re expressing ourselves, and the other thing is we’re trying to get from A to B in some kind of fluid fashion. And sometimes that means we’re going to take detours. And we may play a group of notes that may have no theoretical relevance so to speak. But if you look at the whole statement then you are — hey now I see. And so yeah, you’re absolutely right. You can only analyze this music so much and it was never — this music did not evolve out of academe. That came later. Even classical music, that did not — I mean all the analyzation and stuff, that came later. It was simply creating beautiful art. And that’s what it should be about.
